The just-captured `q` must remain unchanged; the new input values only become candidates for the next negative edge.

Immediately after sampling, before the next edge, `reset` rises to 1 and `d` changes to `0xAB`. The output `q` must still be `0x12`; reset is synchronous, so it does not asynchronously force `q` to `0x34` in the middle of the cycle. At the next sampled negative edge, `reset` is high, so expected `q` becomes `0x34`, not `0xAB`. This single example separates three common checker mistakes: updating expected `q` on a mid-cycle input change, treating reset as asynchronous, and capturing `d` when reset should dominate.

Power-up is unspecified, so the checker must not assume `q` starts at zero, at `0x34`, or at any other value. The reset value `0x34` is a capture value at a negative edge, not a power-on default. Any initial expected value must be established by the stimulus, by an explicit sampled reset, or by a known initialization event in the testbench. In prose, the useful discipline is: track row-start inputs, inputs at the sampled negative edge, post-sampling changes, and carried inputs into the next row separately.
